answer_text:
The polynomial depends on the eigenvalues of \(T\), which are not stated in the prompt. In the usual version of this problem, \(T\) is a projection, i.e. \(T^2=T\), with \(\operatorname{rank}(T)=r\). Then

\[
V=\operatorname{im}(T)\oplus \ker(T),\qquad 
\dim \operatorname{im}(T)=r,\quad \dim \ker(T)=n-r.
\]

On \(\operatorname{im}(T)\), \(T\) acts like \(1\); on \(\ker(T)\), \(T\) acts like \(0\). To make \(g(T)\) have eigenvalue \(11\) on \(\operatorname{im}(T)\) and eigenvalue \(17\) on \(\ker(T)\), we need

\[
g(1)=11,\qquad g(0)=17.
\]

A linear polynomial satisfying these is

\[
g(t)=17-6t.
\]

Indeed,

\[
g(T)=17I-6T,
\]

so on \(\operatorname{im}(T)\),

\[
g(T)v=(17-6)v=11v,
\]

and on \(\ker(T)\),

\[
g(T)v=17v.
\]

Thus \(g(T)\) has eigenvalues \(11\) and \(17\) with multiplicities \(r\) and \(n-r\), respectively, so its characteristic polynomial is

\[
(11-t)^r(17-t)^{n-r}.
\]

Therefore, for the standard projection case,

\[
\boxed{g(t)=17-6t}.
\]

If instead the omitted hypothesis was \(T^2=I\) with \(\dim E_1(T)=r\) and \(\dim E_{-1}(T)=n-r\), then one would need \(g(1)=11\) and \(g(-1)=17\), giving

\[
g(t)=14-3t.
\]
